title: Throughput-oriented design: optimize for total work per watt, not single-thread speed
where_in_paper: Introduction / 'Design philosophy' or motivation section at the start of the paper
decision: Optimize Niagara for high throughput on commercial server workloads (web, transaction processing) measured per watt, rather than for peak single-thread performance.
alternatives_or_rejected: The paper explicitly contrasts this against a conventional high-frequency, deeply-pipelined, out-of-order superscalar design that maximizes single-thread speed but consumes disproportionate power for diminishing returns on throughput workloads.
rationale: Server workloads are largely throughput-bound and highly threaded; aggressive single-thread ILP techniques (deep out-of-order, wide issue, large caches tuned for latency) spend transistors and watts for gains that the workload does not exploit.
outcome: Niagara uses many simple cores with hardware thread support; the paper reports the resulting thread density and watts-per-thread as the key win.

title: Eight 4-thread cores rather than fewer complex cores or more single-threaded cores
decision: Use eight simple in-order cores, each supporting four hardware threads, instead of (a) fewer but more aggressive cores or (b) more cores each with only one thread.
alternatives_or_rejected: The paper argues against widening cores (more issue width, out-of-order) because the cost is high and the benefit on the target workloads is limited; it also argues that single-threaded cores would underutilize execution units given the workloads' memory latency and stall behavior.
rationale: Multithreading per core hides memory and pipeline stalls, raising utilization of a simple pipeline; eight such cores expose enough thread-level parallelism for the workload mix without paying the area/power cost of complex cores.
outcome: Paper presents 8 cores x 4 threads = 32 hardware threads supported concurrently; reports that this keeps pipelines busy across thread switches.

title: Small per-core L1 I-cache and unified on-chip L2 shared across all cores
decision: Equip each core with a small low-latency L1 (modest I-cache and D-cache) and pool a shared on-chip L2 cache across all eight cores.
alternatives_or_rejected: The paper argues against giving each core a large private L2; per-core latency-optimized L2s would waste area and would not let threads on different cores share working-set lines.
rationale: Server workloads exhibit significant inter-thread working-set overlap, and a shared L2 lets a single fetched line serve multiple cores; per-core L1s remain small to keep hit latency short.
outcome: Paper reports a shared L2 with an interconnect that lets fetch L2 lines without going off-chip; describes this as key to keeping traffic local.

title: Hardware thread selection / priority scheme for fine-grained (round-robin) thread scheduling
where_in_paper: Multithreading / pipeline section, near discussion of thread switching
decision: Use fine-grained (every-cycle) thread switching with a round-robin style priority among the four threads per core to keep the pipeline fed when the currently selected thread stalls.
alternatives_or_rejected: The paper argues against coarse-grained switching alone stall periods would leave the pipeline idle) and against relying purely on software/OS to hide latency (because stalls here are too short and frequent).
rationale: Per-cycle switch with a fixed priority among a small thread is simple, fair, and effective at filling stalls caused by cache misses or long-latency events; the simplicity keeps the pipeline short.
outcome: Paper reports that the switch policy is what keeps the simple in-order pipeline's utilization high; integrates with the branch / miss handling it describes.

title: Integrated on-chip memory controller and I/O, eliminating an external northbridge
where_in_paper: Chip-level integration / I/O section, often near the end of the paper
decision: Integrate the memory controller and key I/O interfaces directly on the Niagara die rather than relying on an external chipset/bridge for memory access.
alternatives_or_rejected: The paper contrasts this against a conventional approach where the CPU relies on an external memory controller/bridge, which adds latency and pins and does not match the throughput target.
rationale: Throughput-oriented workloads generate many independent memory streams from many threads; integrating the controller shortens the path to DRAM and lets the chip aggregate bandwidth the threads can request.
outcome: Paper presents the integrated controller as enabling the bandwidth and latency that make the thread-heavy design viable; described as one of the chip's headline features.
